nodes.label: Delozier-Blanchet et al. (1989) described 2 brothers with severe postnatal growth retardation and severe mental retardation, extreme microcephaly, obesity developing during infancy, microgonadism, and a characteristic amphora-shaped facies. Neurologic examination showed hypertonia, hyperreflexia, nystagmus, and extremely irritable and agitated behavior. The first child died at 4.5 years and had also had neonatal hypoglycemia and chronic constipation.

Delozier-Blanchet et al. (1989) noted that the cause was unknown. They suggested recessive inheritance, either autosomal or X-linked, and considered an X-linked recessive gene especially tempting because of the importance of the X chromosome in mental retardation.

Delozier-Blanchet et al. (1989) found that the brothers most resembled patients with Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome. However, their dwarfism and mental retardation were much more severe than in any reported BFL patient, and their neurologic and dysmorphic features differed significantly. The authors considered either a particularly severe, possibly allelic, variant of BFL or a previously undescribed disorder.

Steinmüller et al. (1998) described a previously unrecognized X-linked mental retardation syndrome in a large 3-generation family, with clinical hallmarks of mental retardation, epileptic seizures, hypogonadism and hypogenitalism, microcephaly, and obesity. Patients had a life expectancy of less than 2 years.

Steinmüller et al. (1998) designated the condition by the acronym MEHMO, based on its major clinical features: mental retardation, epileptic seizures, hypogonadism and hypogenitalism, microcephaly, and obesity.
By haplotype and 2-point linkage analyses in a large 3-generation family, Steinmüller et al. (1998) mapped the MEHMO disease locus to Xp21.1-p22.13, in a region flanked by CYBB and DXS365.
DeLozier-Blanchet et al. (1999) assigned the disease locus for MEHMO syndrome to chromosome Xp21.1-p22.13.
DeLozier-Blanchet et al. (1999) described MEHMO as a new syndrome made up of mental retardation, epileptic seizures, hypogonadism and hypogenitalism, microcephaly, and obesity.

Leshinsky-Silver et al. (2002) described a child with MEHMO syndrome (mental retardation, epileptic seizures, hypogenitalism, microcephaly, and obesity) who also had lactic acidosis. Histologic staining of a muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial proliferation and lipid storage. Electron microscopy showed abnormal, enlarged mitochondria with concentric cristae and electron-dense bodies.

Leshinsky-Silver et al. (2002) found markedly reduced activities of complexes I, III, and IV of the mitochondrial electron transport chain in a muscle biopsy from a child with MEHMO syndrome. They concluded that this was the first identification of MEHMO as a mitochondrial disorder, and one of the very few X-linked mitochondrial syndromes.
Decreased activity of mitochondrial complex I
Decreased activity of mitochondrial complex III

Borck et al. (2012) described a family of Moroccan Jewish ancestry in the maternal line in which 3 males had an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome with moderate-to-severe ID, microcephaly, short stature, and facial dysmorphism. Individual features included cleft lip and palate and behavioral impairment (III:1), generalized seizures (III:2), and postpubertal microgenitalism and obesity (II:3). Brain MRI showed a thin corpus callosum and enlarged lateral ventricles. The parents I.1 and I.2 were first cousins.
By targeted linkage analysis using 18 X-chromosomal STR markers in 10 family members, Borck et al. (2012) identified a 10.7-Mb candidate region at Xp22.11-p21.1 containing 35 annotated genes.

In the 3 affected males of a Moroccan Jewish family with XLID and microcephaly, Borck et al. (2012) identified a hemizygous c.665T>C (p.Ile222Thr) missense mutation in the EIF2S3 gene by exome sequencing within the linkage region, confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The mutation cosegregated with the disorder, female carriers were heterozygous, and it was absent from 188 Moroccan Jewish control X chromosomes, dbSNP132, 1000 Genomes, and >8,000 ESP alleles. Ile222 lies in the GTP-binding domain and is strictly conserved in animals.

Borck et al. (2012) found no additional EIF2S3 mutations by sequencing all 12 exons in 60 individuals from families with unspecific, potentially X-linked ID, suggesting that EIF2S3 mutations confer a specific phenotype.

Borck et al. (2012) noted a previously reported EIF2S3 missense variant c.451G>C (p.V151L) from an XLID resequencing project, absent from SNP databases and predicted damaging; the orthologous yeast V210L mutation, near the Met-tRNAi binding site, caused defects in growth, GCN4 expression, and start site selection, and the growth defect was suppressed by tRNAi(Met) overexpression, suggesting impaired Met-tRNAi binding.

Borck et al. (2012) found that myc/His6-tagged human eIF2-gamma I222T expressed in HeLa cells pulled down substantially less endogenous eIF2-beta than wildtype, without affecting eIF2-alpha binding, indicating disrupted eIF2 complex integrity. Structural modeling on archaeal aIF2 placed the corresponding residue in the hydrophobic cleft binding eIF2-beta helix alpha-1.

Borck et al. (2012) found that yeast eIF2-gamma with the analogous V281T mutation impaired eIF2-beta binding without affecting growth, whereas V281K nearly abolished eIF2-beta binding and impaired growth. Both mutations increased GCN4-lacZ expression (2.5- and 40-fold) and raised the UUG/AUG initiation ratio 2-3-fold; eIF2-beta overexpression partially suppressed these defects. The authors concluded that the mutation impairs eIF2 integrity, ternary complex function, and start codon fidelity.

Moortgat et al. (2016) described 2 unrelated families with suspected X-linked syndromic intellectual disability in which affected males had severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, growth retardation, and epilepsy.

In affected males from one of 2 families with syndromic X-linked intellectual disability, Moortgat et al. (2016) identified by X-chromosome exome sequencing a hemizygous missense mutation in the EIF2S3 gene, c.777T>G (p.Ile259Met); obligate carrier females were heterozygous.

In affected males from the second family with syndromic X-linked intellectual disability, Moortgat et al. (2016) identified a hemizygous frameshift mutation in the EIF2S3 gene, c.1394_1397del (p.Ile465SerfsTer4); obligate carrier females were heterozygous.

Moortgat et al. (2016) found that morpholino-based knockdown of the zebrafish EIF2S3 ortholog (eif2s3) recapitulated the human microcephaly and short stature phenotype, supporting pathogenicity of the identified variants.

Skopkova et al. (2017) described MEHMO as a rare X-linked syndrome characterized by profound intellectual disability, epilepsy, hypogonadism and hypogenitalism, microcephaly, and obesity. They linked it to mutations in EIF2S3, which encodes the gamma subunit of translation initiation factor eIF2, and placed it among disorders of translation initiation and the integrated stress response.

Skopkova et al. (2017) reported a Slovak boy (family 1) born to nonconsanguineous parents. Microcephaly was detected prenatally, and at birth he had micropenis, cryptorchidism and peripheral hypertonia. He developed drug-resistant partial complex seizures at 4 months, severe developmental delay, central obesity, and non-autoimmune insulin-treated diabetes diagnosed at 10 months. His dysmorphic features included full cheeks, large ears, downturned corners of the mouth, epiblepharon, tapered fingers and talipes. Brain MRI showed delayed myelination that progressed with acute demyelinating changes and cerebral atrophy. Muscle biopsy showed abnormal mitochondria, and seizures and diabetes control worsened during infections. At 5 years his height was -5 SD and his head circumference -8.4 SD.

Skopkova et al. (2017) measured respiratory chain activity in permeabilized muscle fibers from the family 1 proband. Complex II activity was reduced (1.22 vs 3.11 nM/min/mg in controls; P = 0.009), and complex IV activity was normal.
Decreased activity of mitochondrial complex II

Skopkova et al. (2017) reported a second Slovak boy (family 2) from a nonconsanguineous family, with an unaffected mother and no other affected relatives. He had a birth head circumference of -5.1 SD, therapy-resistant seizures from 6 months without an EEG correlate, hypogenitalism, severe developmental delay, central obesity, and dysmorphic features. He had non-autoimmune insulin-treated diabetes from 10 months, and MRI showed delayed myelination. At 3 years he was hypotonic, had no voluntary movements and showed no social interaction.

Skopkova et al. (2017) restudied the German family originally reported by Steinmüller et al. The index patient was diagnosed with microcephaly prenatally and was born at 32 weeks. He had therapy-resistant seizures from 7 weeks, hypogenitalism, severe delay and central obesity. His dysmorphic features included facial telangiectasias, edematous hands and feet, and bilateral talipes. Diabetes was diagnosed at 6 months after a ketoacidotic crisis, and he died at 2 years with refractory seizures. Female carriers in the family were unaffected.
Edema of the dorsum of hands

Skopkova et al. (2017) reported a boy (family 4) of Northern European origin living in the US, born to nonconsanguineous parents. He had microcephaly, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, developmental delay, and obesity that followed a period of failure to thrive. He had no epileptic seizures and his EEG was normal. He also had hypotonia with peripheral spasticity, chronic lung disease, dysphagia, delayed gastric emptying, grade 5 vesicoureteral reflux and congenital scoliosis, but no diabetes.

In affected males from 3 families with MEHMO syndrome (2 Slovak families and the German family originally reported by Steinmüller et al.), Skopkova et al. (2017) used whole-exome or X-chromosome exome sequencing to identify the same hemizygous 4-bp deletion in the last exon of EIF2S3 (c.1394_1397delTCAA). The deletion causes a frameshift (p.Ile465Serfs*4) that replaces the last 8 amino acids with 3 different ones. It segregated with the disease, was absent from dbSNP and ExAC, and had a CADD score of 35.

In the boy from family 4, who had a milder phenotype, Skopkova et al. (2017) identified by trio exome sequencing a hemizygous missense variant in EIF2S3 (c.324T>A, p.Ser108Arg) that he inherited from his healthy mother. The variant changes a serine that is conserved down to Drosophila, was absent from dbSNP and ExAC, and had a CADD score of 24. The equivalent yeast mutation (Asp167Arg) had no effect, and the healthy brother could not be tested, so the authors classified the variant as of unknown significance.

The 3 families carrying c.1394_1397delTCAA reported no common ancestors, and identity-by-descent analysis excluded relationships closer than about fourth-degree cousins. However, Skopkova et al. (2017) found that comparison of sequencing data and haplotypes suggested a founder effect with more distant relatedness.

Skopkova et al. (2017) found no EIF2S3 coding variants in the 2 previously reported MEHMO families (DeLozier-Blanchet et al. and Leshinsky-Silver et al.). The Leshinsky-Silver patient carried a SERAC1 p.Tyr430X mutation. The authors suggested that in the DeLozier-Blanchet family the defect could lie outside the regions covered by exome sequencing, or in another gene that mimics MEHMO.

Skopkova et al. (2017) built a yeast/human eIF2-gamma chimera to model the variant. The chimera carrying Ile465Serfs*4 caused slow growth that was worse at 37 degrees C, and it was expressed at normal protein levels. It derepressed GCN4-lacZ expression nearly 3-fold and doubled the UUG/AUG initiation ratio, effects comparable to the XLID-associated Val281Thr mutation. These results indicated that the C-terminal mutation impairs eIF2 function.

In patient fibroblasts, Skopkova et al. (2017) showed that the C-terminally truncated eIF2-gamma protein is produced. In fibroblasts from a family 3 patient with Ile465Serfs*4, DDIT3 transcript levels were 2.5-fold higher than in controls and CHOP protein was also elevated. This indicated activation of the integrated stress response.

Skopkova et al. (2017) noted that all 4 index patients with the C-terminal frameshift mutation (including a previously reported family) had full MEHMO syndrome. Three of them developed insulin-dependent diabetes in the first year, and none achieved head control, voluntary movement or social interaction. Patients with missense mutations (p.Ser108Arg, p.Ile259Met, p.Ile222Thr) were less severely affected and had only subsets of the features. The authors proposed that more severe EIF2S3 mutations cause full MEHMO and less deleterious ones cause a milder form.

Skopkova et al. (2017) proposed that EIF2S3 mutations, like mutations in the EIF2B genes and PPP1R15B, reduce the activity or availability of the eIF2 ternary complex. They suggested this leads to insufficient protein synthesis and chronically elevated ATF4 and CHOP, causing apoptosis. They also noted that, as in vanishing white matter disease, patient 1's condition worsened markedly during illness.

Gregory et al. (2019) described 3 affected males from a nonconsanguineous white European family: monozygotic twin brothers (III4, III5) and their maternal cousin (III3). They had severe recurrent hypoglycemia, short stature with GH and TSH deficiencies, mild learning difficulties, and an unusual form of glucose dysregulation that fluctuated between hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and postprandial hyperglycemia. Brain MRI showed variable white matter loss and a small anterior pituitary with normal posterior pituitary and stalk. Severe intellectual disability and microcephaly were absent, and all 3 boys attended mainstream school.

Gregory et al. (2019) reported that patient III3 presented with poor feeding and hypoglycemia 18 hours after birth, had total anomalous pulmonary venous return, severe gastroesophageal reflux requiring Nissen fundoplication, GH deficiency, global developmental delay needing 1:1 support, behavioral problems, and mild hepatomegaly. MRI also showed hypoplasia of the corpus callosum and ventricular asymmetry. An OGTT at 8 years showed symptomatic hypoglycemia at 3 hours with inappropriate insulin, suggesting hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.

Gregory et al. (2019) reported that the monozygotic twins (III4, III5) had intestinal lymphonodular hyperplasia, hypoglycemic seizures and GH deficiency at 2 years, central hypothyroidism at 2 years, and microphallus that enlarged on GH therapy; III4 had transient undescended testes. They had delayed speech with mild conductive hearing loss and behavioral and mild learning difficulties. At 10 years they had impaired glucose tolerance with fluctuation between hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, elevated HbA1c, and persisting hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia at 13.6 years; they progressed through puberty spontaneously.

In 3 affected males of a family with hypopituitarism and glucose dysregulation, Gregory et al. (2019) identified by X-exome sequencing a hemizygous c.1294C-T transition in the EIF2S3 gene, resulting in a pro432-to-ser (P432S) substitution at a highly conserved residue in the C-terminal domain of eIF2-gamma. The variant was inherited from heterozygous mothers (sisters), originating from the heterozygous maternal grandmother, and segregated in an X-linked recessive manner over 3 generations. It was absent from ExAC and gnomAD and predicted deleterious.

Gregory et al. (2019) noted that the mother of the twins had secondary amenorrhea with osteoporosis, menarche at 13 years and cessation of periods at 16 years, and a normal brain MRI; the mother of III3 also presented with secondary amenorrhea.

Gregory et al. (2019) screened 103 patients with congenital hypopituitarism (isolated GHD, septooptic dysplasia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism/Kallmann syndrome, multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies) and identified no further EIF2S3 variants; none had glucose dysregulation similar to the index family.

Gregory et al. (2019) found by in situ hybridization that EIF2S3 was expressed in the human embryonic ventral hypothalamus, Rathke's pouch, anterior and posterior pituitary, nasal epithelium progenitors and retina at Carnegie stages 20 and 23, and in the islets of Langerhans of a 13-week fetal pancreas. In a human pancreatic beta-cell line (1.1B4), shRNA knockdown of EIF2S3 by 82% caused significantly increased basal and cytokine-stimulated caspase activity, suggesting increased apoptosis.

Gregory et al. (2019) introduced the yeast equivalent of P432S (P490S, in a locally humanized eIF2-gamma) into yeast. It did not affect growth but caused a modest (~1.7-fold) significant increase in GCN4-lacZ expression, compared with ~11-fold for the I318M equivalent of the I259M mutation, and increased UUG start codon initiation from ~1.6% to 3% of AUG. The authors concluded that P432S modestly impairs eIF2 function and may cause disease by altering the fidelity of start site selection.

Gregory et al. (2019) noted that their patients lacked the microcephaly, epilepsy and obesity that are prominent in previously reported MEHMO patients and had a much milder neurodevelopmental phenotype. They proposed that the milder loss of function of P432S produces a phenotype distinct from classic MEHMO syndrome, and suggested that untreated hypoketotic hypoglycemia may have contributed to the more severe neurodevelopmental impairment and seizures in previously reported cases.

Gregory et al. (2019) treated the patients with recombinant human GH, thyroxine, and diazoxide with chlorothiazide; diazoxide and chlorothiazide were stopped when hyperinsulinism resolved at 7 years, but the twins later had postprandial hyperglycemia and variable fasting hypoglycemia. The boys grew well on GH. The authors suggested that early molecular diagnosis may prevent significant morbidity and neurodevelopmental delay.
